title: What the law asked of the first man, and what the regenerate give
source_text: XV. Nempe lex illa a primo homine postulabat, ut omni cum alacritate atque promptitudine, absque ullo torpore, sive renitentia Deo obsequeretur, & reapse primus homo, quamdiu integer mansit, tale obsequium Deo exhibere poterat: nec tantillum ab ea perfectione recessisset absque vitio & culpa, cujus se in Dei judicio reum constituisset. Quantum vero jam ab ea perfectione absint qui sunt per Christi gratiam renati, testatur cujusque eorum sensus & conscientia. Etenim quum legi divinae obediunt & bene operantur, id non faciunt sine magna difficultate. Prava concupiscentia, quae post acceptam Dei Gratiam in iis manet, quando divino cultui & aliis actibus lege praeceptis vacandum est, multum illis languoris & torporis injicit: quum vero mala vitanda sunt, propensionem & inclinationem in iis ad illa excitat. Unde fit ut in bonis aegre sequantur Spiritus sancti ductum, & in malis aegre avellantur ab illecebris peccatorum. Proindeque nec mala fugiunt, nec bona prosequuntur tanto cum ardore, atque ex tam puro Gloriae Dei zelo, quam lege exigente, homo integer manens id praestare potuisset. Et ita bona eorum opera legi quidem conformia sunt, sed tamen non juxta ἀκρίβειαν illam, quam lex ex prima sua institutione aestimata exigit, & secundum quam homo nondum peccato corruptus, opera sua legi conformare poterat & debebat.
pass_a_gloss: XV. That law namely demanded from the first man, that he should obey God with all eagerness & readiness, without any sluggishness, or resistance, & in fact the first man, as long as he remained upright, could show such obedience to God: nor would he have departed ever so little from that perfection without fault & guilt, of which he would have made himself guilty in God's judgement. But how far those who are regenerate by the grace of Christ are now from that perfection, the sense & conscience of each of them testifies. For when they obey the divine law & do well, they do not do it without great difficulty. Depraved concupiscence, which remains in them after God's Grace has been received, when they must give themselves to divine worship & to other acts commanded by the law, casts much languor & sluggishness upon them: but when evils are to be avoided, it stirs up in them a propensity & inclination towards them. Whence it comes about that in good things they follow the leading of the Holy Spirit with difficulty, & in evil things they are torn away with difficulty from the allurements of sins. And so they neither flee evil, nor pursue good with so much ardour, & from so pure a zeal for God's Glory, as, the law requiring it, man remaining upright could have shown. And thus their good works are indeed conformed to the law, but yet not according to that ἀκρίβειαν, which the law, valued by its first institution, requires, & according to which man not yet corrupted by sin could & ought to conform his works to the law.
pass_b_english: Thesis XV. That law required the first man to obey God with complete eagerness and readiness, without any sluggishness or reluctance. As long as he stayed upright he really could give God that kind of obedience, and he could not have fallen even slightly short of it without a fault that would have made him guilty before God's judgment.

How far the regenerate now are from that perfection, each one's own feelings and conscience bear witness. When they obey God's law and do good, they do it only with great difficulty. The corrupt desire that remains in them after they have received God's grace weighs them down with listlessness and sluggishness when they need to give themselves to worshipping God and to the other acts the law commands; and when evil must be avoided, it stirs up in them a leaning and inclination toward it.

That is why they follow the Holy Spirit's lead toward good only with difficulty, and tear themselves away from the lure of sin only with difficulty. So they do not flee evil or pursue good with the ardour, or from the pure zeal for God's glory, that unfallen man could have shown as the law required.

Their good works do conform to the law, then, but not to the strict exactness (ἀκρίβειαν) the law demands when measured by its original institution, the exactness to which man, before sin corrupted him, could and should have conformed his works.

choices.why: The law as given to the first man, demanding flawless and uninterrupted obedience.
